children: Board room squabbles are not new, but it is not often that a regulator unwittingly becomes a catalyst for one.

Following RBI's September 11, 2026, rejection of Tata Sons' application to surrender its Core Investment Company (CIC) registration, the September 17 board meeting of Tata Sons witnessed a tussle over the listing requirement and the larger management control issue over the extension granted to the present Chairman. The two issues are interlinked and could therefore delay the compliance with the RBI directive if they go to court.
RBI’s long timeline to reach a decision could trigger questions

While the RBI’s right to regulate in this case is indisputable, the fact that it took almost 30 months to reject the Tata Sons application for de-registration, using an extended interpretation of the public fund norm, leaves its action open to debate. In fact, but for the interpretation of this norm, Tata Sons seemed to have a good case.
It is likely that this may turn out to be Tatas’ principal defence if it goes to court, especially the question of disproportionality between the rule and the objective sought to be achieved.
Compulsory listing is the issue

Interestingly there are over half a dozen non-financial business groups in the list of CIC-NBFCs, but except Tata Sons, all the others fall under the Middle Layer which does not have this contentious listing requirement of listing. Apart from the listing, there is a capital requirement rule where UL (upper layer)-NBFCs must maintain Equity Tier 1 ratio of 9% in addition to the CRAR of 15%.

There are also some restrictive, bank-equivalent concentration caps in terms of exposure to a single counterparty/group of connected counterparties as a percentage of Tier1 capital. But for the moment, the bone of contention seems to be the compulsory listing.
The legal precedence is clear, RBI is within its rights to regulate

There are many legal issues at stake. The questions of ownership versus control, the validity of board resolutions, articles of association and shareholder rights may be put to the test of law. The question of philanthropic trusts running commercial businesses may not be in question as there are many global examples. But the case for compelling some to go public in the interest of financial stability seems less convincing.

The RBI’s regulatory directive does not seem to be in dispute as its powers to override the Companies Act and regulate corporate behaviour (from sections 45Q and 45-IA of the RBI Act 1934) are well established.

They have been upheld by the judiciary and the Supreme Court even opined that the regulator's "expert judgment" on what constitutes a risk should not be second-guessed by courts. Nevertheless, its directives continue to be subject to intense debate mainly on the grounds of appropriateness and disproportionality.
The case of upper layer-NBFC

The issues arise because the criteria were designed for banking business. The capital-to-risk-weighted-assets, ALM and liquidity guidelines, for instance, are more relevant to a financial entity than for a CIC that only invests to control subsidiaries and does not raise any debt. Likewise, the severe exposure caps for a UL-NBFC, may be perfectly sound for a bank, but could be seen as unduly restrictive for a non-banking CIC set up precisely for that purpose.

In fairness, the RBI’s 50:50 rule (financial assets over 50% of total assets, and income from financial assets over 50% of gross income) weeds out the vast majority of entities from its ambit. The RBI is also aware of the mismatch between the criteria and the business activity and in fact had devised a new category of “Unregistered Type I NBFCs” in April 2026 (for those with assets less ₹1,000 crore, not availing public funds and not having a customer interface) precisely for this purpose. Unfortunately, the extended interpretation of the public funds rule closed the door on Tata Sons.
Risk of regulatory arbitrage

One solution could have been for RBI to tailor the criteria/regulations for non- banking entities but perhaps fears of regulatory arbitrage if it tried to differentiate between a holding company and others and the overarching concern about non-financial corporates trying to operate as surrogate banks must have led to its sticking to the same criteria.
The RBI’s regulatory reach over non-financial entities raises a few other interesting questions. There is an aspect of double regulation which though valid could become a compliance overkill.

Tata Capital, a subsidiary is also regulated by RBI and had in fact gone public to comply with RBI regulations. If and when Tata Sons goes public, it will have to deal with two regulators, namely, RBI and SEBI. While the RBI has been tracking systemic risks from financial interconnectedness in its financial stability report, the issue of supervision often seemed to fall between the cracks when multiple regulators were involved (insurance, securities, banking). This came out sharply during the past crises in the Mutual Fund (MF) industry, when surrogate lending by an MF from its debt fund schemes caused a system-wide liquidity crisis.

It will also be interesting to see how the statutory conflict (between RBI Act and Corporate Law) plays out; under the RBI Act, Tata Sons must go public but that would require a special resolution passed by 75% of the shareholders at an AGM.

In the event of the latter not happening, there could be an impossibility of performance situation. The RBI had faced this problem in the past and the cases relating to Kotak Mahindra Bank, Ujjivan SF Bank, Equitas SF Bank or Bandhan SF bank come to mind. If a prolonged negotiation with Kotak Mahindra Bank got the latter to submit, it had to apply its powers by freezing the opening of new branches to get Bandhan Bank to comply.

But here it is dealing a national business icon, not a bank, with philanthropic trusts as promoters and it will be interesting to see how RBI proposes to proceed. In any case, it may have to wait till the management problem is resolved which itself could be a prolonged affair in the courts.
(SA Raghu is a columnist who writes on economics, banking and finance.)
Views are personal, and do not represent the stand of this publication.

title: Tata Sons Imbroglio: RBI’s peculiar role
